---
title: Why does AI make mistakes?
summary: Break a fruit sorter on purpose with a wrong label and with missing examples, then fix it.
language: science
shape: 5e
unit: how-ai-learns
order: 5
voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 }
app:
  command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8241
  url: http://127.0.0.1:8241/index.html
  readySelector: "#gpanel"
  layout: full
explainClip:
  query: { code: "@boards.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain }
  caption: "Investigate the model's decision"
  say: "Inspect the clues, then test the prediction."
  clip:
    - caption: { text: "This simple model uses only colour and shape." }
    - wait: 1100
    - caption: { text: "Its prediction is something to check, not automatically accept." }
    - wait: 1100
---
Last lesson you taught a fruit sorter with labelled examples. Today you will **break it on purpose**. Finding out how a model goes wrong is one of the best ways to understand it.

The sorter is a simple teaching model, not a neural network. It looks at the examples closest to a new fruit and copies their label.

## Engage: what could go wrong?

```step
stage: predict
check:
  type: predict
  q: "The sorter's program works perfectly. Can it still give a wrong answer?"
  options: ["No: if the program works, the answer is right", "Yes: if its examples or labels are wrong or missing", "Only if the computer is broken"]
  actual: "Yes. The program can follow its steps perfectly and still be wrong, because it learns from examples, and examples can be wrong or missing."
```

## Explore: fool the sorter

```step
stage: run
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#explore", height: 680 }
tasks:
  - check: { type: board, text: "Make the sorter call a yellow, long fruit an apple.", when: "a = 1" }
    hint: ["Which examples are closest to a yellow, long fruit?", "Press Swap label on the yellow, long examples, then test a yellow, long fruit."]
  - check: { type: board, text: "With every label correct, make the sorter get a fruit wrong or unsure.", when: "b = 1" }
    hint: ["Press Restore original examples first, so every label is correct. Which kind of fruit has only one example?", "Remove the yellow, round apple, then test a yellow, round fruit."]
  - check: { type: board, text: "Fix the sorter so it gets a fruit right that it got wrong.", when: "x = 1" }
    hint: "Press Restore original examples, then test the same fruit again."
```

In the board's pretend world, every **long** fruit is a banana and every **round** fruit is an apple. The board tells you when the sorter is right or wrong.

### A wrong label

Use **Swap label** to give some examples the wrong answer. Then test a yellow, long fruit. Rows with a wrong label turn pink.

### Missing examples

Press **Restore original examples**, so every label is correct. Now use **Remove** to take examples away. Can you make the sorter wrong, or unsure, without any wrong labels?

### Fix it

Put the examples right again. Test the fruit it got wrong. Is it right now?

## Explain: two kinds of mistake

```step
stage: investigate
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "You swapped two banana labels to 'apple'. Now the sorter calls a yellow, long fruit an apple. What caused the mistake?"
      options: ["Wrong labels: it copied the answers it was taught", "Missing examples: it had nothing close to compare with", "The program has a bug"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "The yellow, long examples were still there. Their labels were wrong.", "The program did exactly what it always does. The examples changed."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "You removed the only yellow, round example. Every label is still correct. Now a yellow, round fruit is called a banana. What caused it?"
      options: ["Missing examples: its closest examples were now yellow bananas", "Wrong labels: some answers were wrong", "Yellow, round fruit can't be sorted"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Every label was correct. Something else was missing.", "With the yellow, round apple back, it sorts these fine."]
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I can explain one mistake caused by a wrong label and one caused by missing examples." }
```

A model can go wrong in at least two ways.

- **Wrong labels.** If examples are labelled wrongly, the model learns the wrong answer. Real AI is often trained on labels made quickly by people, and some are wrong.
- **Missing examples.** If no examples are like the new case, the model guesses from ones that are not really similar. Real AI can struggle with things that were rare or missing in its training data. Generalising to new cases only works as well as the examples it learned from.

In both cases, the program worked. The **examples** were the problem.

### The swapped labels

Which kind of mistake was this?

### The removed examples

Which kind of mistake was this?

### Explain it

Use one of your own board tests as an example.

## Elaborate: more examples, fewer mistakes?

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#explore", height: 680 }
check: { type: reflect, text: "I tested whether more examples fix both kinds of mistake, and explained what I found." }
```

Swap two banana labels to apple, so the sorter calls a yellow, long fruit an apple. Then **add** three more correct yellow, long banana examples. Test again. Did more correct examples outvote the wrong ones?

Press **Restore original examples**. Remove the yellow, round apple and add three more yellow, long bananas. Test a yellow, round fruit. Did more examples help this time?

**Wider investigation:** a real fruit can be green **and** long: an unripe banana. What extra clue, or what kind of example, would help? Would it guarantee the right answer?

## Elaborate: when the missing group is people

```step
stage: modify
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "The app's program has no bug. Why does it mishear Year 7 students more than adults?"
      options: ["Year 7 voices were missing or rare in its examples", "Year 7 students speak less clearly", "Someone gave it wrong labels on purpose"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "The app had few young voices to compare with. That is the same mistake as your sorter with no yellow, round apples.", "Nothing says the labels were wrong. Think about which examples it had."]
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Would this help the app work for Year 7 students?"
      options: ["Helps", "Does not help"]
      items:
        - ["Add many recordings of Year 7 voices", "Helps", "This adds the missing group."]
        - ["Add even more adult voices", "Does not help", "Like your extra bananas: more of the same doesn't fill the gap."]
        - ["Test how well it works for each age group before using it", "Helps", "Testing each group shows who it fails before anyone relies on it."]
        - ["Ask Year 7 students to speak like adults", "Does not help", "The problem is the examples, not the students."]
        - ["Run it on a faster computer", "Does not help", "Speed doesn't change what it learned from."]
```

A school tries a made-up reading app that listens to students read aloud. It learned from thousands of recordings, but almost all of them were adults. It works well for teachers. It often mishears Year 7 students.

### Why it happens

This is your sorter's **missing examples** mistake. This time the missing group is people.

When a model works worse for a group because that group was missing or rare in its examples, we call it **bias**. The program can be fine. The examples are not.

### What would help?

Sort each idea.

## Evaluate: what would you check?

```step
stage: info
check:
  type: question
  q: "A photo app labels a photo of a husky as 'wolf'. Every training label was checked by experts. What is the most likely cause?"
  options: ["It had few examples like this one, so it compared it with wolves", "Some of its labels were wrong", "The app's program crashed"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "The labels were checked. Think about which examples it may have been missing.", "A crash would give no answer, not a wrong one."]
```

Without the board, write: **The sorter got it wrong when … because … . To fix it, I would … .**

## Learning with AI: when the answer is wrong

When an AI assistant gives you a wrong answer, it isn't always because it is "broken". It may have learned from wrong examples, or seen few examples like your question. So ask: *Is my question unusual? Could it have learned this wrong?* Then check with a source you trust.

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I can name two reasons an AI could be wrong even when its program works." }
```

```teacher
summary: Students break a working fruit sorter on purpose, once with a wrong
  label and once by removing examples, then fix it and explain what went wrong.
time: 30
goals:
  - I can make a model give a wrong answer by changing its examples or labels.
  - I can explain the difference between a mistake caused by a wrong label and
    one caused by missing examples.
  - I can say what I would check when an AI gets something wrong.
  - I can explain bias as a model working worse for a group that was missing or
    rare in its examples.
before: >
  Bias step (18 Oct 2026): the reading app is made up, so the lesson makes no
  statistical claim. It names bias as a consequence of generalising from missing
  examples (a technical idea first; the planned Who Does AI Affect? course takes
  up fairness and who is affected). Keep discussion on examples and testing, not
  on judging any real group's speech.

  Last lesson students taught the sorter. This lesson they break it. The board's
  mistakes mode adds a Swap label button and three challenges (wrong label,
  missing examples, fix it); each ticks when a test shows it.

  In the board's pretend world every long fruit is a banana and every round
  fruit is an apple, so the board can say "right" or "wrong". Real fruit is
  messier: say so.

  The sorter copies the label of its nearest examples. It is a transparent
  teaching model, not a neural network.

  No account or online tool is needed.
running:
  - "Engage: ask what could make a sorter wrong before anyone touches the board."
  - "Explore: let students find their own way to fool it; collect the different
    ways on the board."
  - "Explain: sort the ways into 'wrong labels' and 'missing examples'; ask
    which one a bigger dataset would not fix."
  - "Elaborate: connect to real systems: labels are often made by people,
    quickly, and some kinds of case are missing."
struggle: "Students may think a model that is wrong must be broken or badly
  programmed. Here the program is fine: the examples are the problem."
stuck:
  - see: A student cannot make the sorter wrong.
    ask: Which examples does a yellow, long fruit sit closest to?
    fix: Swap the label on one or two yellow, long examples, then test a yellow,
      long fruit again.
  - see: A student fixes the sorter by changing the test fruit instead of the
      examples.
    ask: Did the sorter change, or just the question you asked it?
    fix: Keep the same test fruit and change only the examples.
support: Do the wrong-label challenge together first, then let students try the
  missing-examples one.
stretch: Find the fewest changes that fool the sorter. Why does removing one
  example sometimes make no difference?
leads: Unit 2, lesson 3 shows how a model can weigh several clues at once.
exit:
  q: A sorter with all correct labels still calls a fruit wrongly. What is the
    most likely reason?
  a: Its examples do not cover that kind of fruit well, so its nearest examples
    point the wrong way.
explain: >
  A model learns from its examples. A wrong label teaches it the wrong answer.
  Missing examples leave it guessing from cases that are not like the new one.
  The program can be working perfectly and the answer can still be wrong.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: If an AI's program has no bugs, whose fault is a wrong answer?
    prompts:
      - The people who chose the examples, the people who labelled them, or the
        people who use the answer?
      - Does it matter if no one meant it to go wrong?
    notes: Responsibility can be shared. Avoid settling on one answer; the lesson
      shows two different causes (a wrong label, missing examples) with no bug
      in either.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: discussion
      title: Can perfect code be wrong?
      minutes: 3
      do: >
        Vote with a hand: can a program with no bugs still give a wrong answer?
        Two students explain opposite votes.
      notes: Don't resolve it yet; the Explore step does.
    - at: run
      kind: activity
      title: Break it on purpose
      minutes: 6
      do: >
        Use paper example cards. Group A swaps one banana's label to 'apple'.
        Group B removes every yellow, round card. Each group then sorts the same
        mystery fruit and reports its answer.
      notes: "Two groups, two different mistakes, same 'program' (the rule they
        followed). Name them: wrong label, missing examples."
    - at: modify
      kind: discussion
      title: When the missing group is people
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        A voice app misheard Year 7 students more than adults. In threes: what
        examples were probably missing, and what would you ask the makers to
        check?
      notes: Keep the focus on who was missing from the examples, not on blaming
        individuals. Link to the inquiry question.
```
